title: Biochemical approach for isolation of polyadenylated RNAs with bound proteins from yeast
author: Matia-González, Jabre, et al.

steps.title: Establish RNase‑free workspace
steps.instruction: Work in an RNase‑free environment: clean surfaces with RNase‑ZAP™ or equivalent, wear gloves, use sterile filter tips and RNase‑free low‑binding tubes, and keep all lysates and samples on ice to minimise RNase, DNase and protease activity.

steps.title: Prepare YPD agar and streak yeast
steps.instruction: Autoclave YPD medium, pour plates, and streak ~10–20 µL of glycerol‑stock S. cerevisiae (e.g., BY4741) onto a YPD agar plate using a sterile loop; keep the stock on ice and return to –80 °C after use. Incubate plates upside‑down at 30 °C in the dark until colonies reach 0.2–0.3 cm (≈2 days). Plates may be stored at 4 °C for up to 3 months.

substeps.instruction: Turn on a Bunsen burner (updraft effective within 30–70 cm).

steps.title: Overnight pre‑culture
steps.instruction: Pick one colony from the YPD plate and inoculate 20 mL YPD in a sterile 100 mL Erlenmeyer flask. Grow overnight (12–14 h) at 30 °C with shaking at 220 rpm (use at least a 1:5 flask‑to‑culture volume ratio).

steps.title: Scale‑up culture to mid‑log phase
steps.instruction: Dilute the overnight culture into 500 mL YPD in a sterile 3 L Erlenmeyer flask to an initial OD₆₀₀ ≈0.1 and grow at 30 °C, 220 rpm until OD₆₀₀ ≈0.6 (≈3 h 30 min; doubling time ≈90 min). Measure OD₆₀₀ with a spectrophotometer set to 600 nm, using a 1 mL YPD blank (A = 0.00). Perform a 1:10 dilution of the pre‑culture to calculate the volume needed for the inoculation.

substeps.instruction: Take OD₆₀₀ readings every 2 h until ≈0.4, then every 30 min.
Optional stress: at OD₆₀₀ ≈ 0.6 add 0.5 mM H₂O₂ and incubate 15 min to induce mild oxidative stress.

steps.title: UV crosslink cells
steps.instruction: Harvest cells at OD₆₀₀ ≈ 0.6 by centrifugation at 3,000 × g for 3 min at room temperature (22–25 °C). Wash three times with 25 mL PBS (room temperature), collecting cells by the same centrifugation. Resuspend the pellet in 15 mL 1× PBS, spread the suspension evenly in a 15 cm petri dish to form a thin layer, place the dish on ice in a 254 nm UV‑crosslinker, and expose to 3 × 400 mJ cm⁻² UV pulses with two 2‑min ice breaks and gentle mixing between exposures. Harvest the crosslinked cells by centrifugation at 3,000 × g for 3 min at 4 °C, then snap‑freeze pellets in liquid nitrogen. Store pellets at –80 °C for up to two months.

substeps.instruction: Critical: Ensure an even thin layer of cells for uniform UV exposure.

steps.title: Prepare cell lysate
steps.instruction: Resuspend frozen pellets on ice in 4 mL lysis buffer, pipette up/down, and split into four 2 mL safe‑lock microcentrifuge tubes. Add glass beads to each tube at 2/3 of the tube volume. Balance the tubes in a TissueLyser adapter and lyse at 30 Hz for 10 min at 4 °C (preferably in a cold room).

steps.title: Clarify lysate by sequential centrifugation
steps.instruction: Centrifuge lysates sequentially: 3,000 × g for 3 min, then 5,000 × g for 5 min, and finally 10,000 × g for 5 min, all at 4 °C. After each spin, carefully transfer the supernatant to a fresh tube with a filter tip, avoiding pellet contamination. After the final spin, combine all supernatants in a 15 mL Corning centrifuge tube.

steps.title: Determine protein concentration
steps.instruction: Measure protein concentration of the combined lysate using a Bradford assay with BSA as standard, following the manufacturer’s instructions (typical yield ≈3.5 mg mL⁻¹).

steps.title: Concentrate protein and aliquot
steps.instruction: Concentrate the lysate to ≈10 mg mL⁻¹ using an Amicon® Ultra‑4 10 kDa centrifugal filter unit, following the manufacturer’s protocol; do not let the final volume drop below 1.2 mL. Prepare 500 µL aliquots containing ≈5 mg protein (≈10 mg mL⁻¹) in Eppendorf Protein LoBind tubes. Keep 75 µL of the extract as reference (50 µL for RNA quality assessment, remainder for protein analysis). Store lysates on ice for immediate use or snap‑freeze and keep at –80 °C for up to one month.

substeps.instruction: Check that the filter membrane is not damaged by pipette tips; re‑quantify protein after concentration.

steps.title: Assess RNA integrity (QC step)
steps.instruction: Isolate total RNA from 50 µL of the concentrated extract using the ZR RNA MiniPrep kit per the manufacturer’s protocol. Quantify RNA with a Nanodrop ND‑2000 and load 1 µg onto a 1 % agarose gel stained with peqGREEN RNA/DNA dye. Typical yield is ≈30 µg total RNA from 50 µL extract. Verify that rRNA bands are intact; degraded RNA (e.g., after RNase ONE treatment) should appear as a smear.

substeps.instruction: Optional negative control: treat an aliquot with RNase ONE, then repeat RNA isolation and gel analysis to confirm complete degradation.

description: The protocol describes the specific steps for poly(A) RNA interactome capture (RIC) from UV-irradiated budding yeast cells grown in rich media (Yeast-Peptone-Dextrose (YPD)). The protocol has also been applied to cells treated with 0.5 mM hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) as a stress reagent for induction of mild-oxidative stress (Matia-González et al., 2021). The procedure is based on the capture of poly(A) RNA, a major component of it comprising mRNAs. Hence, the protocol presented here is preferred for investigation of mRNA regulation executed by mRNA binding proteins (mRBPs) that mediate the processing of mRNA precursors (pre-mRNAs) in the nucleus, the export and localization of mRNAs to different subcellular locations in the cytoplasm, and the translation and eventual decay of mRNAs (Singh et al., 2015). We wish to note that there are alternative RIC protocols aimed at isolation of proteins associated with total RNA from yeast (including highly abundant ribosomal RNAs, tRNAs) and are based on organic phase extraction (Queiroz et al., 2019) or the use of silica beads (Shchepachev et al., 2019). In any cases, cells are exposed to UV-irradiation to promote covalent crosslinks between the RNA and proteins in close proximity. However, it should be noted that UV-irradiation of cells can also lead to protein-protein and protein-DNA crosslink, a possibility to be considered for interpretation of the data. Yeast lysates contain a substantial amount of enzymatic activities (e.g., RNases, DNases, and proteases). Cell lysates and samples should therefore be kept on ice, which substantially reduces enzymatic activity. It is also necessary to add RNase and protease inhibitors to buffers/samples immediately before use according to the suggestions given in the protocol. Furthermore, we recommend using sterile filter tips and RNase-free tubes with low RNA/protein binding capacities.
